edition.locus: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia (archive bub_gb_DY2xvRwPetMC), Latin column, chapter IV, printed pp. 44-45 (PDF pages 68-69)

source_text:
In corpore quidem nostro Animam esse superius ostensum est: quomodo autem sit in corpore, cognoscere oportet. Nam si illi ita adiacet, ut lapis lapidi: sequitur, quod corpus sit Anima, nec totum corpus animatum esse, cum parti cuidam solum adhaereat. Sin autem cum corpore mista, confusaque sit; e propria Animae ratione deiecta, multis partibus constabit, nec simplex erit. Quod enim multarum est partium, divisibile est ac dissolubile: quod autem potest dividi, compositum est: compositum vero tripliciter dividi potest. Corpus autem adiunctum corpori, molem auget: Anima vero in corpore existens, illud non tumidum, sed vivum potius reddit. Non igitur corpus, sed incorporea est Anima.

Ad haec, si corpus esset Anima, aut extrinsecus, aut intrinsecus moveretur. Non autem extrinsecus movetur: non enim impulsione, neque tractione movetur, ut inanimata: neque intrinsecus movetur, sicut animata. Absurdum enim est, Animam animae dicere. Non ergo Anima est corpus: incorporea igitur.

Et rursus, si corpus est Anima, etiam qualitates habet quae percipiuntur sensibus, et nutritur: sed non nutritur. Quod si nutritur, non corporee nutritur, ut corpus, sed incorporee: nam ratione et verbo nutritur: non igitur sensibiles qualitates habet: Neque enim oculis cernitur iustitia, neque fortitudo, neque alia eius generis, quae sunt Animae qualitates: quapropter corpus non est anima: incorporea igitur.

Praeterea, cum omnis substantia corporea, in animatam vel inanimatam dividatur; dicant qui Animam corpus esse affirmant, animatamne dici eam velint, an inanimatam.

Denique, si corpus omne colorem, quantitatem, et figuram habet: nihil autem eiusmodi in Anima conspicitur: non igitur anima est corpus.
thought_title: That the soul is not a body
orientation: Five arguments show that the soul is not a body: how it is present in the body, how it moves, how it is nourished, the dilemma of whether it is animate, and its lack of color, size and shape.
pass_a_gloss: That the soul is in our body was shown above (superius ostensum est); but how it is in the body we must learn (cognoscere oportet). For if it lies beside (adiacet) it as stone beside stone (lapis lapidi), it follows that the soul is a body, and that the whole body is not animate (animatum), since it adheres (adhaereat) only to some part. But if it is mixed and blended (mista confusaque) with the body, cast down (deiecta) from the soul's own proper account (propria Animae ratione), it will consist (constabit) of many parts and will not be simple (simplex). For what is of many parts is divisible and dissoluble (divisibile ac dissolubile); what can be divided is composite (compositum); and the composite can be divided threefold (tripliciter). But a body added to a body increases the mass (molem auget); whereas the soul existing in the body renders it not swollen (tumidum) but rather living (vivum). Therefore the soul is not a body but incorporeal (incorporea). In addition, if the soul were a body, it would be moved either from outside or from inside. But it is not moved from outside, for it is not moved by pushing nor by drawing, as inanimate things; nor is it moved from inside, as animate things (animata). For it is absurd (absurdum) to say a soul of the soul (animam animae). Therefore the soul is not a body; incorporeal therefore. And again, if the soul is a body, it also has qualities (qualitates) which are perceived by the senses, and it is nourished (nutritur); but it is not nourished. And if it is nourished, it is not nourished bodily (corporee), as a body, but incorporeally (incorporee); for it is nourished by reason and word (ratione et verbo). Therefore it does not have sensible qualities (sensibiles qualitates). For justice is not seen with the eyes, nor courage, nor others of that kind, which are qualities of the soul. Wherefore the soul is not a body; incorporeal therefore. Besides, since every bodily substance (substantia corporea) is divided into animate or inanimate, let those who affirm the soul to be a body say whether they wish it to be called animate or inanimate. Finally, if every body has color, quantity and shape (colorem, quantitatem, figuram), but nothing of this kind is observed (conspicitur) in the soul, then the soul is not a body.

choices.why: 'ratio' taken as the account or definition of a soul; sense uncertain, nothing added.
rejected: thrown out of the soul's own nature

choices.english: can be divided in three ways
choices.why: Probably extension in three dimensions, but the Latin does not say so.
rejected: can be divided in length, breadth and depth

choices.why: Close rendering; a possible echo of Matthew 4:4 is left uncited as uncertain.
rejected: it feeds on reason and speech

pass_b_english: We have shown above that the soul is in our body; we must now learn how it is in the body. For if it lies against the body as one stone lies against another, it follows that the soul is a body, and that not the whole body is animate, since the soul clings only to some part of it. But if it is mixed and blended with the body, it will have fallen from what properly makes it a soul; it will consist of many parts and will not be simple. For what has many parts can be divided and dissolved; what can be divided is composite; and what is composite can be divided in three ways. Again, a body joined to a body increases its bulk; but the soul, being in the body, does not make it swell, but rather makes it alive. The soul, therefore, is not a body but incorporeal.

Besides this, if the soul were a body, it would be moved either from outside or from within. But it is not moved from outside, for it is moved neither by pushing nor by pulling, as inanimate things are. Nor is it moved from within, as animate things are, for it is absurd to speak of a soul of the soul. The soul, then, is not a body; it is therefore incorporeal.

Again, if the soul is a body, it also has qualities that the senses perceive, and it is nourished. But it is not nourished. But if it is nourished, it is not nourished in a bodily way, as a body is, but in an incorporeal way, for it is nourished by reason and by the word. It does not, then, have qualities the senses can perceive. For justice is not seen with the eyes, nor courage, nor anything else of that kind, and these are the qualities of the soul. The soul, therefore, is not a body; it is incorporeal.
Further, since every bodily substance is divided into animate and inanimate, let those who claim that the soul is a body tell us whether they want it called animate or inanimate.
Finally, if every body has color, quantity and shape, and nothing of the kind is seen in the soul, then the soul is not a body.
notes: Edition chapter IV ('An incorporea sit Anima').
Five print paragraphs kept as five English paragraphs.
Doubtful reading: 'e propria Animae ratione deiecta' rendered 'it will have fallen from what properly makes it a soul' (ratio = the account or definition of a soul); sense uncertain.
'corpus sit Anima' taken as 'the soul is a body'.

'tripliciter dividi potest' rendered literally 'can be divided in three ways'; the underlying idea is probably extension in three dimensions (length, breadth, depth), but the Latin does not say so and the English does not add it.
'Absurdum ... Animam animae dicere': to say the soul moves from within like animate things would give the soul a soul of its own.

'ratione et verbo nutritur': possible echo of Matthew 4:4 / Deuteronomy 8:3 ('not by bread alone ... but by every word'); left uncited because the link is uncertain and the work by Tatian's request avoids Scripture testimonies.
The edition's margin note 'al. corpoream' at 'Animam corpus esse' (reading uncertain) would give 'claim that the soul is bodily'; same sense, not adopted.
The fourth argument ends as a question to the opponents, as printed; nothing supplied.
